description: Objective:To design and realize a first European portable self-calibrated SI-traceable Rydberg atom-based Electric field probe.Description:Accurate measurement of electric fields is crucial for the development and operation of RF communicationsystems, particularly in space missions. Conventional antennas need fine calibration for high-integrity reception. The calibration is performed by placing uncalibrated antennas in a known EM (electromagnetic) environment that is measured via a well-calibrated antenna which creates a dependency. Whereas Rydberg based receivers allow precise measurements of RF signals which is directly related to Planck's constant and hence can self-calibrate by relying on SI (international system of units)-traceable atomic standards The activity aims to develop a portable, self-calibrated Rydberg atom based electric field probe.The probe is based on the interaction of RF-fields with Rydberg atoms, where alkali atoms are excited opticallyto Rydberg states and the applied RF-field alters the resonant state of the atoms. For this probe, the Rydbergatoms are placed in a glass vapor cell. The vapor cell acts like an RF-to-optical transducer, converting an RF Efield to an optical frequency response. The probe utilizes the concept of Electromagnetic Induced Transition (EIT), where the RF transition in the four-level atomic system causes a split of the transition spectrum for the pump laser. This splitting is measured and is directly proportional to the applied RF field amplitude. Therefore, by measuring this splitting, we get a direct measurement of the RF E-field strength. This technique could allow traceable measurements over a large frequency band including 1-500GHz. The new approach has the following benefits: 1) it will allow direct SI units linked RF E-field measurements, 2) It is self-calibrating due to atomic resonances, 3) it will provide RF field measurements independent of current techniques, 4) the probe will not perturb the field during the measurement, since no metal is present in the probe.This activity encompasses the following tasks:-Assessment of different Rydberg atom-based methods of detection of RF fields.- Requirement consolidation and performance assessment.- Detailed concept design with analysis of critical functions.- Development of the breadboard and verification in relevant environment.- Development of a technology roadmap for an EQM.
title: PORTABLE SELF-CALIBRATED RYDBERG ELECTRIC FIELD PROBE FOR ANTENNA MEASUREMENTS - EXPRO+

description: Objective: To develop and assess Mars guided entry and control algorithms for the entry and descent phases, including smart parachute or retro-propulsion triggering, and implement them as on-board software.Description: Entry, descent, and landing (EDL) of Mars missions are critical for ensuring the successful deployment of precision landers for human and robotic exploration. In particular, the entry and descent phases involve complex aero/thermodynamics which require precise guidance and control to achieve the proper conditions for deploying parachutes or for activating supersonic retro-propulsion. In fact, most of the dispersions occur in these phases, and while various approaches for guided-entry algorithms (reference path tracking, predictor-corrector methods, and model-basedtechniques) offer different advantages, all of these come at the expense of many challenges and trade-offs. This activity aims to trade-off different approaches for the design of Mars guided entry and control algorithms, in combination with smart parachute and/orsupersonic retro-propulsion triggering (when applicable), to reduce the dispersions that shall be removed by the landing phase. By assessing their performance through high fidelity Model-in-the-loop (MIL) simulations, the most effective algorithms can be identifiedand considered for numerically efficient and robust implementation as on-board guidance software. The added value includes improvedlanding precision, enhanced safety, and optimized entry and descent performance, which are all essential for the success of future Mars missions. The performance of the developed algorithms will be evaluated via high-fidelity dynamical simulations, while portability to flight processors will be assessed through profiling of the developed guidance  control algorithms. This activity encompasses the following tasks: - Consolidation/review of the proofs-of-concept and state-of-the-art of guided entry. - Definition of requirements, operational scenarios, use-cases, and preliminary validation and verification (VV) plan. - Detailed development of guidance and control algorithms with focus on performance, and optimization for embeddability. - Implementation and performance assessment ofalgorithms in an End-to-End Mars landing EDL simulator. - VV campaign of the proposed solutions and algorithms. - Assessment of computational performance on a space-graded processor through profiling. - Study synthesis, and recommendations for a technology roadmap to increase TRL.
title: GUIDANCE CONTROL ENTRY TECHNOLOGY FOR MARS PRECISION LANDING - EXPRO+

description: Objective:To identify, demonstrate, and implement recycling of high-value scrap into quality feedstock for additivemanufacturing of components for space applications.Description:As the demand for spacecraft, satellites and launch systems grows, so too does the consumption of criticalraw materials - many of which are finite, expensive and environmentally burdensome to extract. Recycling andreusing materials offer a strategic solution, reducing dependency on virgin resources, lowering carbonemissions and enhancing supply chain resilience. By integrating recycled materials into components, thespace sector can not only reduce its environmental footprint but also pioneer circular economy practices that will be essential for long-term sustainability - both on Earth and in future off-world manufacturing ecosystems.Furthermore, materials like titanium, aluminium and nickel alloys are in high demand in the space sector, yetthese materials are primarily imported from non-European sources. Developing local recycling solutions for high-value, critical materials is a vital step towards achieving European material self-sufficiency, especially in the current geopolitical and economic context. Potentially significant sources of scrap include machining waste (e.g. swarf, off cuts) and unused powder from additive manufacturing. Scrapped parts due to manufacturing defects are expected to be a secondary, less frequent, source but may become more relevant in the context of out-of-earth manufacturing. The space sector should also consider sourcing waste/scrap materials from other industries (e.g. aviation, automotive).The activity will start by identifying hot spots of high-value material scrap across European manufacturing(space and non-space). A hot spot in this context would be defined as materials with high volume of scrap,high material value/cost, raw material being sourced outside Europe, and high demand by the space industry.Selected scrap will then be processed into quality raw materials, tested, and used to produce and evaluate ademonstrator part to be defined based on a business case (e.g. bracket, fuel tank).This activity encompasses the following tasks:- Identify sources of scrap material, material types relevant for space, and their possible use; down-selection of the most interesting cases (including economic, ecological and technical factors).- Develop processing route(s) for high-value material waste identified in the first task to transform into highquality raw materials for use as space hardware. This will most likely require dedicated alloy development to factor in what properties and quality can be realistically extracted from recycled materials.- Develop the advanced manufacturing process(es) for the use of "up-cycled" materials, considering theinfluence of impurities, potential development of detrimental phases, etc.- Test the produced material on a sample level (material characteristics, mechanical properties, etc.).- Design and manufacture a relevant spacedemonstrator part for subsequent testing to check compliance with relevant functional requirements.- Provide guidance on how to design components produced from recycled materials, seeking to identifypotential trade-offs between quality requirements, safety factors, cost and lead time.Deliverables: Breadboard, Report
title: ADVANCED SUSTAINABLE MANUFACTURING OF SPACE-QUALIFIED COMPONENTS FROM RECYCLED HIGH-VALUE FEEDSTOCK - EXPRO+

description: The Agency seeks to assess the applicability and operational potential of a multi-moment, multi-fluid modelling approach for forecasting and nowcasting the Earth's magnetospheric space weather environment. While current operational systems predominantly rely on global MHD models and fully kinetic approaches remain computationally challenging for routine use, this activity aims to demonstrate whether a multi-fluid framework can provide an effective balance between physical realism and operational performance. Bidders are expected to employ real observational data for model verification, validation, calibration, and performance enhancement, investigating techniques such as data assimilation, data-driven boundary conditions, and other observation-informed methods to improve forecasting capability and scientific fidelity. The activity should include comprehensive testing against measurements and reference models, the assessment of computational performance and operational suitability, and the quantification of forecasting skill for key space weather phenomena. The work shall identify the strengths, limitations, and maturity of the approach, while establishing a clear roadmap towards a future three-dimensional global magnetospheric forecasting capability that can operate faster than real time and support advanced operational space weather services.
title: HE-SWE-03B - GLOBAL MULTI-MOMENT MULTI-FLUID MODEL OF THE MAGNETOSPHERE

description: The main objective of this activity is to comprehensively gather, analyse and consolidate the requirements and specifications for afuture concept of a Measurement Command  Control (MCC) system intended to support ESA propulsion test facilities[ID2.1][ID2.2][ID2.3] for systems and subsystems in a five- to ten-year timeframe. The main use case of such an MCC will be for larger test bench facilities such as the P5 at DLR Lampoldshausen and PF50 at Vernon (hundreds of simultaneous measurements within a large frequency spectrum) but shall be highly adaptable to other similar benches. The activity shall identify innovative technologies, architectural concepts, to support the following objectives:Improve Operational efficiency, maintainability, scalability and performance;SupportStandardization;Ensure energy efficiency for Sustainability purposesReduce Recurring Costs.Subsequently, the study aims to formulate a comprehensive concept for the future MCC, including preliminary system requirements, architectural definition, innovativefeatures, and an assessment of existing and emerging solutions and suppliers ideally from ESA Member States. Thus, the study shall assess the availability and maturity of the required technologies within the European ecosystem, identify potential capability gaps,and recommend developments needed to strengthen European technological autonomy, resilience, and sovereignty in this strategic domain. The resulting concept shall establish the foundations for future procurement and implementation activities across ESA propulsiontest facilities.[ID3.1][ID3.2][ID3.3] Particular attention shall be given to disruptive concepts and architectural evolutions capable of delivering a substantial leap in the bench capabilities with respect to the given objectives.

description: Objective:  To develop a space proven NV-Centred Diamond magnetometer with reduced SWaP. Description:  Magnetic field measurements from low Earth orbit are important for understanding Earth's magnetosphere, monitoring of space weather, and studying geophysical processes. These measurements provide insights into solar-terrestrial interactions and help mitigate risks to both orbital infrastructure and terrestrial systems. NV -centres magnetometers are recent developments that have been successfully implemented on the ISS. Next to their scientific interest, one of their applications lays in using the magnetic field for AOCS purposes in space. Using a magnetic map, the full attitude of the spacecraft can be followed. This has been demonstrated during the first Ariane launch where one of these systems could follow the first minutes of the trajectory of the rocket. There is now the need to further develop such system to allow them to be utilized for navigation of spacecrafts or on other bodies (which have a magnetic field) with a specific focus on reduction of size and mass of the instrument to be integrated to AOCS system. The development shall be focused on miniaturisation and reduction of resources and on increasing the resolution of the magnetometers to pT.  This activity encompasses the following tasks:  - Consolidation of technical requirements given application in miniature quantum devices and preliminary design.- Detailed design of the magnetometer. - Manufacturing, integration and functional verification. - Test campaign, outcomes and development plan to qualification. Deliverables: Breadboard, Reports
title: MINIATURIZATION OF NITROGEN-VACANCY CENTER-BASED MAGNETOMETERS - EXPRO+

description: Objective:To characterise spacecraft materials that minimise atmospheric impacts during re-entry.Description:ESA's Green Agendaand Ecodesign Policy require that the environmental impacts of all space missions andprogrammes are assessed and reduced across their full life cycle. Launch and spacecraft re-entry effects onthe atmosphere are known gaps to fulfil these requirements. This results in significant uncertainty andsystematic exclusion of such effects when developing materials on the basis of sustainable performance.Previous and ongoing Discovery activities, Insights into the Chemistry of Atmospheric Re-entry of JunkedSpacecraft (ICARUS) and Impacts of space Debris ablation on Earth's Atmospheric System (IDEAS), havehighlighted the potential importance of ablation products in the atmosphere while established initial modellingapproaches and experimental validation capabilities.The proposed activity addresses this critical knowledge gap by developing a consolidated experimental andmodelling framework to characterise emissionsfrom spacecraft re-entry and integrate these into atmosphericand design assessment tools. This will enable the incorporation of atmospheric impacts into Life CycleAssessment (LCA) and support both Ecodesign and Design-for-Demise (D4D) decision making. Such aframework would be the first worldwide.The activity encompasses the following tasks:- Identify representative launcher and spacecraft demise-critical materials as well as Space Debris Particles(SPSs)- Propose material characterization factors (e.g. Ozon Depletion metrics, radiative forcing proxies) andassociated quantification methodology- Refine methods to allow observation and characterization of particles generated during the vaporizationphase of selected materials- Demonstrate validation tests under realistic atmospheric re-entry conditions (e.g. Thermal, pressure andflow conditions) measuring and linking ablation fluxes to downstream chemical compositions- Parametrization and modelling of datasets for integration into re-entry and atmospheric chemistryclimatemodels-Define uncertainty and applicability ranges for model use- Formulate recommendations for standardised testing procedures to support the continuous developmentand population of material datasets.Procurement Policy: C(3) = Activity restricted to SME  RD organisations, preferably in cooperation. For additional information please go to:http://www.esa.int/About_Us/Business_with_ESA/Small_and_Medium_Sized_Enterprises/Opportunities_for_SMEs/Procurement_policy_on_fair_access_for_SMEs_-_the_C1-C4_Clauses
title: MATERIALS FOR SUSTAINABLE ATMOSPHERIC RE-ENTRY - EXPRO+

description: Objective:To develop and test a model for a digital twin of attitude and orbit control system (AOCS) sensors as well as toassess compatibility of this multi-physics model-based digital twin with on-board self-calibration employing datadriven techniques and withthe simplification of ground verification processes of new satellite platforms.Description:Advances in model based engineering and digital twin (DT) development has led to growth in the interest of multiphysic modelling of space systems, including, for example, AOCS sensors. The AOCS sensor DTs includefunctional and performance behaviour, complemented by physical behaviour (thermal, power, electronic, etc.), as well as failure and degradation modes. This detailed modelling is based on analytic and background suppliermodels. The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) / machine learning (ML) combined techniques, potentiallyaugmented with analytical a priori knowledge, offer the potential to improve the overall accuracy and validity ofthis modelling, together with a specific interest for statistical interpretation in the case of mass production (sensors for constellations, for example, gyros, star trackers, sun sensors). These new engineering techniques aimed at better fidelity in the AOCS sensor modelling offer the prospect of extending the benefits to on-board performance, for example, by adapting these techniques to the ultimate AOCS sensor calibration: self-calibration on board the spacecraft (e.g. constellation or low-cost platform). The following techniques and use cases will be studied:- Digital Twin for AOCS sensors, preferably from sensors used on platform series: architecture; interoperabilityneeds, multi-physic modelling trade-off and key components; use of data-driven techniques (AI/ML) to populate the DT models; statistical interpretation and validation of AOCS sensor performance (mass manufacturing, groundself-calibration based on sample measurements and statisticextrapolation).- Use of ground models and knowledge for on-board self-calibration; data fusion techniques for on-board use to consolidate ground self-calibration with flight measurements, autonomously; autonomous verification of on-board self-calibration (fault detection).This activity will bring tools, methods, and processes for increasing the end-to-end autonomous handling of AOCS sensorsin the platform development and verification chain. It includes predictive maintenance monitoring to inform on the overall health status and to prevent anomalies/failures. This activity aims at providing digital data and models to improve knowledge of the units in flight, allowing correction and improvement by the supplier and better integration in model-based system engineering (MBSE) or digital production.This activity encompasses the following tasks:- Define the system into which the deliverable items will be integrated, establish the end user requirements andquantify the advantages of utilising the new items with respect to state-of-the-art alternatives.- Define a complete, self-standing and traceable set of technical requirements for the deliverable items.- Select the technical baseline that offers the best potential to achieve the activity objectives.- Detailed design and demonstrate, by appropriate analyses, simulations, tests or other means, that it cansatisfy the technical requirements.- Establish all detailed plans necessary to successfully implement and test the deliverable items and verify theircompliance to the technical specifications.- Implement the deliverable items, quantify their performances by means of a suitable test campaign anddemonstrate compliance to the technical requirements.
title: DIGITAL TWIN OF ATTITUDE AND ORBIT SENSORS - EXPRO+

description: Summary Description The proposed activity is will support the preparation for the ERASE Phase A. ERASE aims to prepare the removalof large, non-cooperative and unprepared objects in low Earth orbit, initially considering Metop and Sentinel-1 targets (starting with METOP-A and S1B, both being decommissioned), thereby supporting ESA's Space Safety Programme and the transition towards a circular economy in space. This activity will establish and demonstrate ground-based laser-ranging measurement, modelling and analysis capabilities to characterise the attitude state and tumbling behaviour of non-cooperative, unprepared targets, with initial focus on Metop and Sentinel-1 targets. The output is essential and urgent for the ERASE Phase A study. Without this information available at the start of Phase A, there is a risk that the technical feasibility of the mission is incorrectly assessed. The target spin rate is adesign driver for the servicer delta-V and operations timeline, the relative navigation subsystem, and the robotic capture sizing and loads. The spin-axis orientation drives the safe approach direction and the capture strategy. In addition, the probability of very low spin-rate cases must be understood, as such cases may lead to long durations in unfavourable attitude conditions for target power generation, thermal control and ground contact. The challenge is that the targets are not prepared with cooperative markers or laser retro-reflectors that would facilitate attitude reconstruction. The attitude state must therefore be reconstructed from non-cooperative laser-ranging observables, making use of time-of-flight/range measurements, return-signal characteristics, pass geometry, target geometry, known or estimated surface properties, and attitude-dynamics modelling. Where beneficial, the laser-ranging data maybe complemented by passive optical or radar observations.The activity will assess the feasibility, achievable accuracy and uncertainty of attitude determination and dynamics-based propagation from ground. It will characterise and propagate target dynamics, in particular spin rate and spin-axis orientation, and will provide statistically meaningful uncertainty envelopes for ERASE Phase A design trade-offs. The activity will also prepare the capability to perform repeated attitude characterisation campaigns in support of ERASE. The attitude state of non-cooperative targets may evolve over time due to environmental torques and target-specific dynamics; therefore, measurements may be required not only during the present feasibility phase, but also before launch, to confirm that the target conditions remain within the design assumptions, and potentially at intermediate points during mission preparation. A dedicated task will assess the applicability of the developed measurement and modelling methods to a broader range of large, unprepared, non-cooperative low Earth orbit targets beyond Metop and Sentinel-1, identifying the key target properties, observation conditions and limitations that determine feasibility.
title: MEASUREMENT AND MODELLING OF THE ATTITUDE OF METOP AND SENTINEL 1 TO PREPARE FOR ERASE PHASE A - EXPRO+

description: To consolidate alternative solutions for on-board loss minimization. To develop the prototypes of the most relevant solutions identified, to confirm the predicted performance. To provide road-map to flight models. The state of art TTC Sub-System architectures for Science and Exploration missions are nowadays quite complex. In order to allow communications during all mission phases, several antennas are needed in combination with redundant High Power Amplifiers (HPA) and transponders (DST). The interconnection among these components is accomplished by the RF Distribution Unit (RFDU), which has to guarantee the maximum degree of reconfigurability and reliability to failures. In addition, it has also to implement the necessary filtering action, to allow full duplex communications. Its design is therefore quite complex encompassing the use of several switches, Diplexers, Filters and interconnecting waveguides (WG) runs. The latter can be quite long as they have to reach antennas which are typically far from the location of the rest of the TTC subsystem. All this results in high losses with RF power reduction in transmission and increased noise figure in reception.The design solutions used so far in the frame of ESA projects are quite recurrent with no major improvements in the last decades. As shown in a TTC Sub-System architecture survey carried out in 2017, different approaches exist, as identified for example by other agencies and already flown successfully in the past years. For a complex RFDU as used in Deep Space missions, we can consider RF path losses in the order of 1 to 3 dB in X-band and 3 to 4 dB in Ka-band, with significant impacts in terms of data return (up to50% reduction) and in terms of spacecraft recovery possibilities in case of anomalies (increasedoperations complexity and limitation on maximum achievable distance). Therefore, there is a clear need for loss reduction in the RFDU paths, through the implementation of novel solutions. A study is on-going to consolidate the possible alternative subsystem Architectures, and define relevant requirements. This will be completed in early 2024, but its conclusions need to be consolidated by experimental results. The activity shall focus on the specification, detailed design, development and tests of prototypes of the components which will have the most significant impact on the TTC subsystem performance and whose feasibility has to be demonstrated. Three main items have been already identified, which may need to be completed by additional technologies as an outcome of the on-going study:- Receiving only antenna with integrated low-noise-amplifier (LNA) and downconverter (D/C), with a possible alternative for a receiving and transmitting solution;- High-gain-antenna dual-band feed including receiving LNA and D/C, and with direct interface to power amplifier;- Transponder front-end to manage the interfaces with new antennas designs.Tasks:1. Consolidation of requirements and design2. Design and manufacturing of bread-boards3. Testing of bread-boards4. Development plan for flight models.
title: IMPROVED TTC SUB-SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE - EXPRO PLUS

description: Objectives: The objective of this activity is to develop a system simulator for testing the RF links of multi satellite missions. The focus of the simulator should be the modelling of a full set of satellite and laned assets transmitters and receivers with their precise orbit determination around different bodies of the solar system (e.g. Earth, Moon, Mars).Description: There is a high interest in the development of cluster of data relay satellites for planetary exploration and navigation. There are different studies and developments ongoing related to this concept both for Moon and Mars. Such a simulator system for Moon and Mars is considered an asset to support the development of this cluster missions and to support the development and test of the user terminals in an operating environment.The objective of the activity is hence to develop a RF simulator of a data relay system. The simulator shall be able to interface via RF either with a user terminal unit or with a data relay unit and to: Model full satellite's cluster transmitters and receivers. Model user terminals' transmitters and receivers. Emulate the user terminal spacecraft dynamic motion on planet surface, orbit, or during descent and ascent from the surface: Doppler, Doppler rate and delay. Emulate the relay satellite dynamic motion in orbit: Doppler, Doppler rate and delay. Emulate transmitter and receiver antenna gain and phase patterns of the relay satellite and of the user spacecraft host. Emulate the interference generated by the multiple transmitters of the cluster. Emulate multipath effects. Emulate any atmospheric attenuation or delay effects (for Mars case). Emulate the (two way) range measurement function of the relay link to characterize the performance and functionality.The RF relay simulator shall emulate the signals of each satellite of the cluster in both Sband and K-band in a modular fashion (i.e. S-band module independent from K-band module). The data relay RF simulator system shall employ software in the loop and hardware in the loop techniques to allow the user to design the test scenarios and to control external hardware blocks. The main goal is to have full control of all aspects of the useroperating environment, to enable exact repeatability of the test and to allow the application of systematic errors or incidents that are normally impossible to verify or not tested during the RF compatibility tests. The Emulation of the relay satellites shall be configurable to emulate different relay systems such as different (type of) Moon or Mars scenario.The following tasks are foreseen in this activity: Revision and consolidation of requirements. Architectural and detailed design, including the design of the simulator system at system level and building block level. The detailed requirements for each buildingblock of the system should be derived. It shall be determined if each building block need to be developed or if there are COTS blocks that can be embedded. Implementation of the hardware and software needed to constitute the system simulator prototype. Test and demonstration of the simulator.Deliverables: Hardware prototype, Software, Report.
title: DATA RELAY RF SIMULATOR SYSTEM - EXPRO PLUS (RE-ISSUE)

description: Objective: The objective of this activity is to develop and test a maritime laser communication terminal prototype to enable optical communication links between aship-based and a space-based laser terminals.TargetedImprovements:Enhance the reliability and stability of a laser communication terminal (LCT) in maritime environments for optical satellite communication. This will resultin a reliable and resilient system for bidirectional ship-space links.Description: While Laser Communication Terminals (LCTs) are being explored for aeronautical and land-mobile sectors, their use in maritime-satellite link applicationsremains untapped. Maritime LaserCommunication Terminal (MLCT) systems offer significant advantages, including secure communications (resilienceto jamming and low probability of interception), high data rates, direct line-of-sight links, which can enhance connectivity for ships but are not available yetin ESA Member States or Canada.This activity will develop and test MLCT prototype for maritime communication applications. It will assess the state-of-the-art for maritime LCTs andevaluate the constraints imposed by dynamic maritime environments, such as sea waves. Following this analysis, existing Pointing, Acquisition, andTracking (PAT) mechanisms, optical head mechanical designand optical communication systems will be benchmarked, and one will be selected andoptimised for effective performance in maritimeconditions. A prototype MLCT will be developed with Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) specifications closeto a final product, ensuring compatibility with current and future planned space LCTs. The MLCT shall be designed for manufacturability at a competitivecommercial cost. The possibility of a test to be conducted with a satellite LCT should be explored

description: Objective: The objective of this activity is to develop a 664 GHz direct detection receiver using innovative packaging techniques for future ultra-compact array instruments.Description: Future array instruments and ultra-compact payload instruments require ultra-compact receiver integrating all RF (Radio Frequency) functions with very small SWaP (Size, Weight and Power), removing complex mechanical and electrical interfaces such as standard waveguide flanges and DC/IF (Direct Current/Intermediate Frequency) coaxial connectors. Novel silicon micromachining techniques are key-enablers to develop ultra-compact RF front-end by integrating in a High-Aspect-Ratio silicon-wafer stack all the key components required to achieve state-of-the-art performance, including high-gain antenna, RF LNA MMIC (Microwave Monolithically Integrated Circuit), RF filters, diode detector, video amplifier and associated DC electronics.This activity aims to develop an integrated 664 GHz Direct Detection Receiver, including a novel high-gain flat-antenna, RF LNA MMIC, a narrow-bandpass filter, and a zero-bias detector with integrated video-amplifier. The developed receiver will be tested radiometrically, including beam pattern measurement, Noise Figure, Short-Term-Gain-Stability, and Gain response over temperature. This activity encompasses the following tasks: - Design of an integrated direct detection receiver operating at 664 GHz. - Investigation ofsilicon-micromachined fabrication and packaging techniques for all critical RF elements: flat-antenna, waveguide active (LNA) and passive (filter) devices, RF/IF/DC interconnections. - Manufacturing and testing of a breadboard model. - Development plan and future roadmap.

description: The increase in small satellite missions has intensified the need for compliance to international space debris de-orbiting requirements. To meet these requirements CubeSat-class missions frequently rely on their primary On-Board Computer (OBC) and Electrical Power Subsystem (EPS) to activate disposal mechanisms, however deployment and late-mission failures; such as battery degradation, bus freeze, or cyber compromise; can prevent successful disposal execution.This activity addresses this gap through the development of the Secure Autonomous Disposal Interface and Safety Module: a standardised, independent Disposal Trigger Module (DTM) compatible withCubeSat buses from 1U to 16U across a variety of disposal mechanisms. The DTM shall implement two autonomy levels of increasing complexity and prove resilient to spacecraft failures and cyberattacks. The project targets bring the technology to TRL6.
title: S3-CL-06 SECURE AUTONOMOUS DISPOSAL INTERFACE SAFETY MODULE - REISSUED

description: Description:  Currently, debris environment models for cislunar space are very limited as such have been primarily developed for Earth-bound orbits. Such models are a necessary asset for collision/impact risk assessment and traffic coordination. With the expansion of human activities beyond Earth, notably in cislunar space, there is an increasing need for models and tools to support missions. This need is reflected on the latest Space Debris Mitigation requirements for lunar orbits, including disposal and availability of space traffic coordination methods. With various studies having explored disposed objects and debris clouds in cislunar space, the development of such models becomes increasingly feasible. Methods and software tools to perform assessments in Earth orbits exist and are well-used. To ensure safe operations and sustainability in cislunar space, an extended density-based model can be used for risk event statistics, delta-v planning for collision avoidance manoeuvres and reliability assessment due to impacts. The model shall leverage the results of recent studies on debris and clouds around the Moon and build upon the well-established tools andmethodologies for Earth orbits. For the dynamically complex lunar orbits, a long-term propagator is needed to support the characterisation and evolution of the population.   Under this activity, cislunar long-term propagators are aimed to be coupled with break-up, lunar impact, and traffic models to create a consistent debris and dust density map for the cislunar environment. To demonstrate the usability and mission application, the model shall be coupled with collision and impact risk assessment tool and tested on a Lunar mission design.
title: T311-900SD DEBRIS ENVIRONMENT MODELLING IN CIS-LUNAR SPACE (EXPRO+)

description: Increasingly, advances in AI applications, models, and big data capabilities are making their way intoproductive applications. Roadmaps exist to introduce AI technologies into critical functional and operationaldomains. With new technology spin-ins like AI, cybersecurity must be accounted for, considering new attacksurfaces and vulnerabilities. Currently, no specialized approach exists forsystems with AI components,necessitating an ad-hoc approach for each system. To avoid redundant efforts, a coherent security approachfor AI applications in the space domain should be defined. Common mitigation measures for identified threatsand risks related to data and models need to be integrated into the AI lifecycle, ensuring a secure and AIenabledinfrastructure. Systems today demand increased security and even security certification. Whilesecurity approaches for non-AI systems are well understood, AI components introduce new threats. Thisactivity will guide developers in creating secure AI systems and assist project teams with certificationbasesfor AI solutions. Building on previous ESA work where security threats and mitigation measures for spacesystems were identified and considering emerging policies and regulations, this activity will develop an'MLSecOps' framework, i.e. a comprehensive set of practices and tools, processes, and datasets to addressnew vulnerabilities. These will be integrated with operational MLOps infrastructure and validated in a spacesystem context. The targeted space system applications may range from engineering aids to securitymonitoring solutions. The solution will be based on public standards and knowledge bases such as the ENISAreport "Cybersecurity of AI and Standardisation," MITRE ATLAS, and OWASP Gen AI Security Project. Theseoffer a rich list of vulnerabilities and controls without considering the required adaptations for space missionspecifics. This activity will establish a set of practices and createcommon tools for AI systems to providestandardized security features and functions, easing the certification process.
title: GT1I-805GA SECURITY FRAMEWORK FOR AI APPLICATIONS (EXPRO+)

description: This Lunar European Power Pack aims to accelerate the maturation of European thermal control and power systems as well as related electronics equipment enabling lunar night survival and lunar night operations in the frame of the ESA lunar roadmap. The output of the Lunar European Power Pack will be a European lunar end-to-end integrated advanced power pack validated design providing thermal control and power as a service to surface Payloads if integrated in the relevant mission's baseline. To enable sustained surface operations on the Moon, robust and autonomous power and thermal services are essential. These systems must be able to support a range of external clients  including systems and payloads hosted on landers, rovers, surface shelters, or deployed payloads  under harsh lunar conditions, from mid-latitudes to polar regions, ranging from daytime to night survival. The goal is therefore to deliver reliable energy and thermal regulation as a modular service, adaptable to multiple mission profiles and operational needs. Ensuring an efficient service/mass ratio is vital for the affordability and is therefore central to any activity.
title: LUNAR EUROPEAN POWER PACKS: SYSTEM-LEVEL CONCEPT STUDY (E3CX-033) - EXPRO PLUS

description: The ESA Antenna Laboratory operates several unique antenna and RF material measurement facilities, including the Sub-mmWave Scanner(SMS), LORENTZ cryogenic near-field scanner, and CATR Material Characterisation Facility. These facilities support antenna and RF characterisation activities covering a frequency range extending from microwave to sub-millimetre-wave frequencies and are routinely used in support of ESA programmes, technology developments, industrial activities and research campaigns.Operation ofthese facilities relies on dedicated custom-developed software that interfaces with motion control systems, network analysers and auxiliary equipment to perform automated measurements, collect measurement data and generate outputs suitable for post-processing andanalysis. Overthe past decade, this software has evolved through multiple development and maintenance activities, supporting successive laboratory upgrades and increasingly demanding measurement campaigns. The software currently comprises three principal application domains:            SMS scanner control software.            LORENTZ scanner control software.            CATR Material Characterisation control software.In addition, a growing set of shared software components has been introduced to provide common functionality across facilities, including hardware abstraction, configuration management, measurement orchestration, data management and graphical user interfaces. Historically, software development activities were executed through a number of independent projects. Consequently, different facilities evolved at different rates and software versions diverged over time. Recent maintenance activities have established a common software management approach based on GitLab repositories, issue tracking mechanisms and shared software components, improving traceability and maintainability of the software assets. The LORENTZ and CATR applications now share a modern architecture built around common software libraries and hardware abstraction layers. The SMS software remains operational but is based on anearlier architecture and represents the principal remaining source of technical debt within the software suite. Long-term sustainability of the Antenna Laboratory software therefore requires continued maintenance, harmonisation and progressive migration towards acommon software framework.The software environment further depends on several third-party components, including software drivers and interfaces fromKeysight, ACS Motion Control, Trio Motion Technology and other equipment suppliers. Maintaining compatibility withcommercial operating systems, hardware drivers and measurement instruments is therefore an essential part of maintaining the operational capability of the Antenna Laboratory. As several ESA facilities depend on the availability, reliability and traceability of measurement data,particular attention must be given to configuration control, software version management, measurement file compatibility and preservation of laboratory know-how. The software shall therefore be maintained as an operational laboratory asset rather than as a standalone development project.- Objective(s) of the ActivityThe objective of the activity is to ensure the continuous operation, maintenance, evolution and long-term sustainability of the Antenna Laboratory software systems, while preserving compatibility with existing facilities, measurement workflows and historical measurement data.
title: SOFTWARE UPDATES SMS, MATERIAL AND LORENTZ - EXPRO+

description: Objective:To design, manufacture and test a 1m deployable offset fed reflector antenna for small/cube satellites suitable formissions up to Ka-band.Description:A strong need for deployable Ka-band high gain antennas for cubesat and small satellites for various applications (TTC, payload data downlink, black hole observation VLBI (very long baseline interferometry), rain/precipitation observation and more) has been identified, hence, the importance to develop this technology to further maturity, which is currently notavailable in Europe.The antenna to be developed is 1m (scalable up to 3m) diameter deployable reflector antenna in an offsetconfiguration (reduction of aperture blockage) suitable for missions up to Ka-band. An engineering model including the reflector, the boom and the feed will be manufactured and tested demonstrating the critical functions of the element in a relevant environment. The testing will include, as a minimum, surface accuracy measurement after deployment, deployment test in representative environment (TVAC), vibration tests, thermal cycling, RF performance tests, passive intermodulation (PIM) tests at sample level.This activity encompasses the following tasks:- Preliminary design (including de-risking activities of new, modified or unmodified (re-used) modules with lower TRL and/or higher risk)- Detailed design (including de-risking activities of unmodified (re-used) modules with lower TRL and/or higher risk).- Antenna manufacture and integration.- Test campaign and development roadmap.

description: Objective: To develop a breadboard demonstrating single-step waste inhibition and compaction and characterize cross-linked biodegradable materials compatible for this process.Description: Re-supply and waste management are critical components of crewed space exploration. The current waste management approach exposes the crew to (bio)safety risks during the temporary storage period and is unpractical in longer space missions. Generic waste compaction/inhibition technologies of mixed waste materials in space have been generally studied. However, despite promising results on the volume reduction performance, the physical characteristics of the product obtained allow for limited transformation of re-usable resources. To address this, the activity aims to develop a breadboard demonstrating single-step waste inhibition and compaction and characterize cross-linked biodegradable materials compatible for this process. Lastly, there is a benefit in defining new packaging materials, which are biodegradable in the conditions of identified recycling systems and withstand the proposed compaction and inhibition process. The activity includes the following tasks: - Review single-step waste inhibition/compaction methods compatible with resource recovery (e.g. water) and developed biodegradable materials - Trade-off and selection of integrated waste inhibition and compaction processes and compliant packaging/padding materials. - Design and assembly of a breadboard system for single-step waste inhibition and compaction - Test to validate selected single-step waste inhibition and compaction technological modifications and biodegradability of treated packaging material - Developed cross-linking agents to enhance the barrier properties of biodegradable packaging materials, while maintaining biodegradability and process compatibility - Test to validate biodegradability and intended use of developed packaging. - Define a roadmap for technology maturation for integration into an operational system.Deliverables: Breadboard, Report
title: NON-BODY SOLID WASTE COMPACTION AND INHIBITION

description: The Strategic Advocacy Facility is a strategic Action Readiness instrument within ESA's Earth Action framework that enables the translation of EO innovation, science and applications into sustained operational uptake and impact, particularly within the impact finance ecosystem of International Financial Institutions, climate and environmental funds, and developing-country stakeholders. The Facility combines programme-level impact measurement and evidence generation, strategic partnership engagement, institutional advisorysupport, country-level uptake assessment, strategic intelligence, advocacy and communication within a single integrated framework. Building on the legacy and assets of the Global Development Assistance (GDA) programme, it establishes a common Theory of Change, monitoring and evaluation system, stakeholder engagement architecture and learning framework for Earth Action, while creating feedbackloops between implementation, partnerships, communication, programme governance and future RD investments. Through interconnected task setup, the Facility acts as a cross-cutting enabler that strengthens EO adoption, supports partner alignment, captures and communicates evidence of impact, and ensures that Earth Action activities can be scaled, mainstreamed and translated into long-term societal, environmental and development outcomes.

description: ERS-EO Proof of Concept on Critical Infrastructure ManagementThe ERS-EO Element 1 Critical Infrastructure Monitoring Prof of Concept is intended to demonstrate the step improvement for enhanced monitoring and management of critical infrastructure resulting from the effective combination of diverse EO and non-EO capabilities representative of the future Earth Observation Governmental Service (EOGS) capacity.  In particular, the customization and fusion of these capabilities will generate significant improvements in tasking response, persistent data collection, information delivery latency, expanded information content andflexibility and adaptability in response to dynamic situations. In this context, the Critical Infrastructure Monitoring PoC will:Stimulate innovative combinations of public and private EO systems to support improved and more flexible tasking, response latency, persistence and cross-operator cueing;Develop customized workflows connecting satellite operators, non-EO data providers, analytics tool developers and critical infrastructure operators to ensure enhanced capability to detect, characterize, respond to and mitigateemergent threats and anomalies;Verify the improvements achievable over current state of the art with respect to emerging threat detection and mitigation action execution for critical infrastructure operators under realistic operating conditions;With respect to gaps in current capabilities, elaborate technical approaches for their resolution, verify their impact under representative operational environments and conditionsand elaborate a road map for eventual transfer to full operations based on exclusively European technology. description: Objective: To analyse the impacts of fault propagation in spiking neural networks (SNN), propose design mitigation techniques, identify relevant neuromorphic IPs and select a baseline concept for implementation.Description: Future missions, including planetary landing, planetary exploration, docking, debris removal, space situational awareness, in-orbit servicing, etc. will need increased autonomy to address latency issues. This autonomy will rely on AI-driven computer vision and advanced computing capabilities. However,traditional neural network inferences typically require hardware platforms such as FPGAs or GPUs, which may consume anywhere from afew tens of watts to 100 watts. This high-power consumption may necessitate active cooling systems, impacting weight, volume, complexity, and ultimately resulting in additional costs and risks for missions. Safety-critical class 1 missions, including autonomous docking, autonomous landing, and autonomous rover/drone navigation, will require lower power, low footprint (pin count), scalable, and fault-tolerant hardware accelerators. Event-based processing with Neuromorphic technologies, show potential for the future of intelligent sensing, whether it involves event-based cameras, LiDAR, or radar sensors. Neuromorphic technology can address in an effectivemanner the challenge posed by edge AI, sustaining a high processing load, while keeping power consumption low (from few Watts to sub-Watt). Concrete use cases such as, autonomous landing, autonomous docking have been studied, validating Neuromorphic technology through the deployment on commercial device (COTS). Neuromorphic technology is suited for computer vision applications, planned activities should also confirm the suitability for radar as well. Few commercial IPs have shown potential in studies as explained above.However, additional work is needed to adapt a solution for space missions, ensuring low power, scalability, low pin count, and fault tolerance. Leveraging state-of-the-art neuromorphic commercially available IPs, this activity aims to propose a solution that addresses these needs effectively by designing a neuromorphic hardware accelerator using advanced rad hard ASIC technology. This activity encompasses the following tasks: - Hardware accelerator specifications consolidation - selection and product roadmap definition - IP fault mitigation techniques analysis - Hardware accelerator architecture definition - Hardware accelerator design - Hardware accelerator validation / simulation.Procurement Policy: C(1) = Activities in open competition limited to the-non-Large-System Integrators.For additional information please go to:http://www.esa.int/About_Us/Business_with_ESA/Small_and_Medium_Sized_Enterprises/Opportunities_for_SMEs/Procurement_policy_on_fair_access_for_SMEs_-_the_C1-C4_Clauses

description: Objective:To develop, manufacture and test a low-cost, integrated high-Isp air-breathing electric propulsion systemsuitable for drag compensation of High-Aspect Ratio (HAR) small satellites operating in VLEO.Description:Sustainable operations in Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO, below 250 km altitude) are currently constrained bythe propellant mass required to continuously compensate for aerodynamic drag. Air-Breathing ElectricPropulsion (ABEP) offers a potential solution by replacing conventional on-board propellant with atmosphericparticles collected through a suitably designed intake and delivered to Electric Propulsion thrusters for thrustgeneration and drag compensation.Previous ESA and non-ESA studies, supported by early-stage technology development activities, have demonstrated the feasibility of the ABEP concept and its strong potential to enable a range of applications, inparticular Telecommunications (D2D / D2H) and high-resolution Earth Observation missions. To reduce the propulsion effort required to counteract aerodynamic drag and prevent orbital decay, VLEO platforms typically adopt slender spacecraft configurations with optimised drag area, typically based on a High-Aspect Ratio (HAR) topology. This activity specifically addresses ABEP systems designed for such drag-areaoptimisedsmall satellites. The ABEP systems will be capable of operating across varying atmospheric densityand composition regimes, accounting for diurnal and seasonal variability, and across altitudes below 250km.Lifetime assessment is required, including appropriate material selection to withstand high-velocity particleimpacts and Atomic Oxygen (ATOX) exposure.The feasibility of integrated ABEP systems for this class of small satellites has already been demonstrated upto TRL 3. This activity aims to mature the technologyat system level through the design, manufacture, andtesting of a fully integrated ABEP system capable of providing continuous dragcompensation for HAR smallsatellites operating in VLEO. The expected outcome is a validated ABEP system at TRL 4, including intake,thruster, fluidics and Power Processing Unit (PPU). Successful completion of the activity will provide a compact and efficient drag-compensation solution to support sustained VLEO operations and address emerging market needs for future VLEO constellations.The activity encompasses the following tasks:- Consolidation of the ABEP system requirements for a High-Aspect Ratio small satellite.- Design, manufacturing, assembly and integration of a fully integrated ABEP system (including PPU,thruster, intake, fluidics).- Perform a functional verification test and performance mapping at system level in VLEO-representativetest conditions.- Define the thrust control laws for drag compensation based on the results achieved in the test campaign.- Perform a short endurance (250h) test that showcases performance stability and lack of early-life failuremechanisms.
title: LOW-COST, HIGH-ISP, INTEGRATED AIR-BREATHING ELECTRIC PROPULSION SYSTEM FOR HIGH ASPECT RATIO VLEO SMALL SATELLITES - EXPRO+

description: Objective:To develop a cost-competitive solar cell either III-V-based or silicon-based for LEO satellite constellations.Description:The satellite industry is undergoing a major shift from traditional geostationary (GEO) platforms to large-scale lowEarth orbit (LEO) constellations. In this new landscape, solar cell requirements are increasingly driven by the needfor scalability, cost competitiveness, and radiation hardness tailored to the LEO environment. III-V multi-junctionsolar cells remain the benchmark for efficiency and space reliability, but their high cost and manufacturingcomplexity limit their suitability for mass production. In contrast, silicon-based solar cells, widely used in terrestrialsolar arrays, offer a more scalable and cost-efficient option, though they are not optimized for the spaceenvironment and typically have lower radiation resistance. Future development of III-V cells should focus onreducing complexity and cost. For silicon technologies, the priority is improving tolerance to radiation-induceddegradation, which is generally more severe than in III-V cells.Within this activity, it is foreseen to develop one solar cell technology that can support the LEO constellations inview of cost competitiveness and production capability. Technology options for this activity are either III-V-basedor silicon-based, with the following specific objectives: Option 1 - III-V-based technology development, to reduce production costs by up to 50% and doublemanufacturing throughput to meet large-scale deployment needs: there is substantial potential to reduce costsand increase manufacturing throughput by optimizing existing processes or implementing new ones. Potentialstrategies include increasing epitaxial growth rates, integrating terrestrial PV techniques (e.g., screen-printingfor contactmetallization), and replacing photolithography steps with more cost-effective alternatives.For this option, the activity encompasses the following tasks:o Develop an optimized manufacturing route for III-V solar cells, incorporating both improvements tocurrentprocesses and introduction of new techniques.o Fabricate solar cell samples using the newly developed manufacturing process.o Conduct an engineering test campaign to evaluate and validate the electrical and mechanicalperformance of the produced cells.This development stream complements developments performed in the following activity: T703-900EP - HighEfficient Cost-Effective Solar Cells. Option 2 - Silicon-based technology development, with the aim to achieve 21% efficiency at beginning-of-life(BOL) and 18% at end-of-life (EOL) and to improve reliability in the LEO space environment. The developmentactivity will focus on both design innovation and process optimization, aiming to enhance radiation toleranceand thermal cycling robustness while achieving the required beginning-of-life (BOL) and end-of-life (EOL)efficiency targets. For this option, the activity encompasses the following tasks:o Implement cell design optimizations already identified for existing silicon solar cell concepts toimprove radiation resistance to meet the 21% BOL and 18% EOL efficiency targets.o Investigate alternative metallization methods, anti-reflective coatings (ARCs), and interconnectiontechniques to improve thermal cycling robustness.o Explore compatibility of silicon structures with potential self-annealing properties to mitigate radiationinduceddegradation with industrial manufacturing framework.o Validate the final solar cell design through an engineering test campaign.This development stream complements developments performed in the following activity: Spin-indevelopment of terrestrial solar cell technology for constellation applications (ARTES AT 4F.175).
title: COST-COMPETITIVE SOLAR CELL DEVELOPMENT - EXPRO+

description: Objective: To design PNT techniques and algorithms relying on only 1 and 2 LEO satellites in view, based on the optimised fusion ofall the available estimations along time.Description: The use of LEO-based systems on top of current GNSS systems (in MEO orbits) is being considered to improve the achievable user performances, in particular in challenging user scenarios. To ensure that at least3 or 4 satellites are in view by any user on ground, a much larger number of LEO satellites than for MEO is required to be used inthis case. In this context, it is of high interest to investigate techniques exploiting signals received by LEO satellites when only 1 and 2 LEO satellites are in view by a ground user. This would enable, for example, to exploit LEO satellites with reduced constellations with a limited available number of satellites visible, and/or while a full LEO-PNT constellation is still being deployed. Theobjective of this activity is to design PNT techniques and algorithms relying on only 1 and 2 LEO satellites in view,, including transitions between 1 and 2 satellites, based on the optimised fusion of all the available estimations along time, including at least:- ToA (Time-of-Arrival), FoA (Frequency-of-Arrival) and AoA (Angle-of-Arrival)-like estimations; - Multi-epoch / synthetic apertureprocessing solutions exploiting the fast satellite geometry change; and, additionally, if introducing benefits to the above : - Clock coasting; - Inertial sensors measurements; - DEM (Digital Elevation Model)/height sensors ; The suitability of the proposed solutions is aimed to be assessed based both on simulations and real data. This activity encompasses the following tasks: - Define and design innovative techniques and algorithms in the areas identified above; - Develop the required tools/software for the assessment/test of the innovative techniques and algorithms; - Assess/test the different techniques and algorithms in realistic simulated conditions, and with real signals from LEO satellites; - Identify the most promising techniques/algorithms based on the results obtained;- Propose the way-forward to further mature each of the promising techniques/algorithms identified.Procurement Policy: C(2) = Activities in open competition, where a significant participation of non-LSI is requested. description: The increasing deployment of satellites is raising concerns regarding their impact on ground- and space-based astronomical observations and the need to comply with emerging Dark and Quiet Skies (DQS) requirements. However, existing data are limited, fragmented and often unsuitable for consistent spacecraft-level brightness analyses. This activity addresses this gap through the development of a system-integrated European database of optical properties for spacecraft materials with potential observational impacts, including solar arrays, multilayer insulation, thermo-optical coatings, antennas and external optical elements. The activity shall establish the required material datasets, perform dedicated measurement and characterisationcampaigns, and integrate the resulting data into an open-access database supporting DQS compliance assessments and brightness prediction tools. description: ObjectivesDeriving algorithms and their optimal settings for enabling real-time highly accurate and reliable navigation based on GNSS carrier phase measurements exploiting quantum optimization algorithms.DescriptionHigh Accuracy with GNSS requires usage of phase measurements, which are ambiguous. Carrier phase Ambiguity Resolution (AR) is a stochastic process which requires a minimizationsearch for the correct ambiguities which can require a very large search to find the correct solution.In recent years, a series ofquantum algorithms for mathematical optimisation has been formulated which could be exploited to replace the classical approaches, such as those currently in use for GNSS AR. Quantum least squares can be used to perform Integer Least Square minimization, which would speed up the processing time for searching the right solution even in a larger search space. A fast and accurate solution of theGNSS carrier phase AR problem by means of quantum optimisation, in particular, would enable real-time Highly Accurate Reliable and Precise (HARP) positioning based on GNSS carrier phase positioning with integrity capabilities for users, achieving stringent positioning bounding with a very high level of confidence.This activity will define algorithms and their optimal settings for quantum optimization algorithms enabling real-time highly accurate and reliable navigation based on GNSS carrier phase measurements. The activity will rely on the quantum computers or simulators nowadays available to users as free prototypes from various companies, anticipating the advent of Quantum Processing Units which could become operational in the mid to long term.This activity encompasses the following tasks:- Definition of the quantum optimisation algorithms for GNSS AR;- Prototyping of quantum navigation estimator for PPP-AR users;- Prototyping of quantum carrier phase AR and identifying its implication on integrity related to achieving HARP positioning;- Trading off of the number of qubits and the achievable performance.DeliverablesReport, Software

description: The objective of the activity is to develop and implement over-the-air satellite system demonstrators that validate Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface technology developments in realistic conditionsTargeted Improvements:Enabling a variety of integrated terrestrial/satellite 5G/6G use-cases currently not feasible with low-gain user antennas.Description: Integrated terrestrial and satellite networks are considered a promising concept for supporting service demands in 5G and 6G communications. However, there are some fundamental issues to be tackled for seamless integration of terrestrial and satellite networks, especially in the case of mobile users operating in complex environments with low directive antennas. For the satellite link, received signals degrade severely upon arrival at the users due to the long-distance propagation, rain fading effects and blockage by obstacles. Moreover, due to spectrum sharing in the integrated terrestrial-satellite network, the interference mitigation problem between the two systems should be considered jointly to enhance the spectrum efficiency. Recently, reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) technology has drawn much attention due to its capability to enable reconfiguration of the radio propagation environment. This technology is based on large planar surfaces, comprising many passive reflecting elements able to induce a controllable amplitude and/or phase change to the incident signal. By strategically installing RIS (e.g., on building facades or roofs), system capacity, coverage, and/or energy usage can be improved cost-effectively. Standardisation bodies, such as 3GPP or ETSI, are in fact now discussing RIS deployments from the operational and regulatory perspectives. Many developments focused on RIS technology already take place as part of industrial, academic and European Commission activities. These developments have not been demonstrated in an endto-end or system context including both terrestrial and satellite networks, which is paramount for attracting the interest of key stakeholders such as satellite and mobile network operators. To fill this gap, this activity shall develop and implement several over-the-air satellite system demonstrators, validating the outcome of various RIS technology developments in various integrated terrestrial-satellite architectures. As a minimum, the activity shall quantify the benefits of RIS in the following realistic scenarios, with low-gain user antenna: 1) Improved link budged thanks to the enhanced signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at the receiver through the RIS-concatenated channel.2) Enhanced satellite user performance by employing RIS to mitigate inter-system interference in the integrated terrestrial-satellite system.Additional demonstrations can be added as soon as technology developments mature following an agile approach. The activity shall assess all relevant RIS developments and propose convincing demonstrations. The activity shall seek synergies with the ARTES deliverables and testbeds as well as by ongoing RIS projects and provide inputs to the 3GPP relevant standardisation working groups.Procurement Policy:C(1) = Activity restricted to non-prime contractors (incl. SMEs). description: The objective: The objective of the activity is to design, manufacture and test a 12bit direct conversion receiver module covering the full Ka-band with significant reduced power consumption in comparison to current state of the art.Targeted Improvements:- Enabling a European source of low power direct conversion Ka-band receivers.- Factor 5 reduction of power consumption compared to the State of the Art.Description: Today's flexible telecommunication satellites require receivers operating at higher frequencies and over a wider bandwidth than in the past, with a complex RF chain and lossyharnesses. A trend towards highly integrated solutions using direct sampling receivers compatible with Software Defined Radios (SDRs) is one solution, but the power consumption of these direct sampling architectures can be prohibitive for some applications. The available direct conversion receivers in Ku-band and Ka-band have power consumption figuresin excess of several Watts and limited conversion accuracy, constraining the application areas where these could be used for space telecommunication applications. A direct conversion receiver system in a single package integrating the Analog to Digital Converter (ADC) in the advanced semiconductor technology and using a time-interleaved ADCarchitecture can achieve the desired lower power consumption and higher conversion accuracy.This activity will develop a prototype wideband ADC with high-speed track-and-hold circuit, implemented as a System-in-Package (SiP) RF to digital front-end module including digital processing features, operating in upper Ka-band. Available State-of-the-Art low-power wideband ADC will be assessed, and a trade-off analysisperformed to determine the optimum RF chain architecture (including the track-and-hold with digital processing engine and high-speed interfaces) suitable for wideband SDRs operating in full Ka-bandapplications. The breadboard will be designed to meet key performance requirements in terms of power consumption (<500mW per channel), bandwidth, and input frequency. The noise and linearity performance shall be measured to determine suitability for a range of SDR scenarios also considering synchronisation and clock jitter requirements. The breadboard shall be tested in a representative RF chain architecture in a laboratory environment, to demonstrate direct sampling at upper Ka-band frequencies and assess viability for V/W band applications. Additionally, radiation tolerance shall be demonstrated by analysis to assess suitability of the low-power ADC for future applications in space.
title: LOW POWER KA-BAND DIRECT CONVERSION RECEIVER MODULE (ARTES AT 5C.525) - EXPRO+ (ON DELEGATION REQUEST)

description: Objective: The objective of the activity is to develop advanced and post-quantum Subscriber Identity Module (SIMs) for 5G/6G NTN. The focus is to improve user anonymity for robust non-terrestrialnetworks (NTNs) used for governmental applications which have a more urgent need for post-quantum anonymity protection than the commercial market. These SIMs shall implementsecurity improvements of the part of the primary authentication protocol which is implemented in the SIM. Additionally, the corresponding SIM provisioning infrastructure and the corenetwork responsible for the communication with the SIMs will be developed.TargetedImprovements: Enablinga European or Canadian source for robust NTN SIM (Physical Universal Integrated Circuit Card (UICC) or Embedded UICC (eUICC)) for 5G/6G satellite constellation withhardened primary authentication protocolDescription: Current 5G Universal Subscriber Identity Modules (USIMs) to be used in Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN) for Satellite Communication (SATCOM) terminals lack adequate protectionagainst user tracking when assuming a quantum attacker. While 3GPP is working on the migration to post-quantum cryptography, the privacy needs in governmental NTN networks arehigher than in usual mobile networks and regulatory needs will require the full post-Quantum migration as early as 2030 for governmental communication solutions. An appropriatesolution therefore needs to be developed earlier than the 3GPP timeline foresees.The activity will design, develop and test prototypes of advanced 5G/6G USIMs integrating security improvements to the primary authentication protocol (user tracking enhancements inNTNs and anticipated regulatory requirements for post-quantum cryptography), with all components adhering to GSMA/ETSI security standards and targeting Common Criteria evaluationto prepare for future accreditation.The activity will evaluate two implementation paths to address this need: Physical Universal Integrated Circuit Card (UICC) development, potentially as an applet on an existing smartcard platform, or Embedded UICC (eUICC) with appropriate SIM profiles for multi-provider service access. Post-Quantum Key Exchange Management (KEM) implementations on smartcards prove the technical feasibility of implementing such protocols in the UICC approach.The activity will be implemented in a phased approach.The first phase will study the implementation of post quantum security in the authentication protocol and perform a trade-off analysis between the two implementation paths. It will designand develop an initial prototype of the USIM and provisioning infrastructure compatible with standardised 3GPP interfaces between USIM and Mobile Equipment and perform the designof the security functions of the Core network solution to interoperate with the USIM. Phase 1 deliverables consist of architecture and design documents, initial documents to prepare thecertification, software prototype and adapted core network functions to interoperate with the software. The budget for Phase 1 is up to 700 kEuros.In the second phase, the activity will further develop and test the USIM components (UICC or eUICC), create the complete SIM provisioning infrastructure, and develop and test the corenetwork security functionsincluding the Subscriber Identifier De-concealing Function (SIDF) to support enhanced authentication of the USIM to the network. Phase 2 deliverables includethe adaptation of smart card including applet design and SIM printer or chip development for eUICC and refined certification preparation.During the activity, dissemination towards 3GPP standardisation shall be performed to ensure futureindustry adoption.
title: ANONYMITY AND POST QUANTUM SECURITY SUBSCRIBER IDENTITY MODULE (SIM) TECHNOLOGY FOR 5G/6G NTN (ARTES 4.0 SPL 4S 3D.040)

description: The purpose of this activity is to study in detail the system and subsystem requirements for a planetary defence mission that aims at building a space-based infrared telescope dedicated to detection and characterisation of Near-Earth Objects (NEOs) that approach from the direction of the Sun. description: Objective: To develop a miniaturised power supply for arrays of detectors on the payload.Description: Detector arrays on Earth Observation (EO) spacecraft require a dedicated local power regulation for each of the detectors (CMOS or infrared). These local powerregulators ensure the supply of low noise voltage rails with specific sequencing and timing. New technologies such Gallium Nitride High-Electron Mobility transistor (GaN HEM FET) would allow to significantly reduce the size of such power supply hence making the complete system much more compact. This activity aims at miniaturising the DC/DC converter by using GaN FETs and Integrated Components(ICs), providing an efficient yet small converter. Moreover, the switching should be as smooth as possible to avoid synchronisationof all the supplies in a hard switching pattern (which would be detrimental for the overall power system). The overall efficiency and Electro Magnetic Compatibility (EMC) performance shall be significantly improved. Overall, the target power supply is targeted tobe 50% smaller and to have a much reduced Electromagnetic interference (EMI), allowing for improved sensor performance. The activity encompasses the following tasks: - Study and trade-off of the optimum architecture (electrical, mechanical and thermal) - Breadboard of miniaturised power supply - Perform breadboard testingDeliverables: Breadboard, ReportProcurement Policy: C(1) = Activity restricted to non-prime contractors (incl. SMEs).
